sections.h2: Which Lebanon offices share the building at 223 North Spalding Avenue?
sections.html:
Lebanon's county government offices for taxes sit under one address, 223 North Spalding Avenue, so a Marion County owner can finish most paperwork in a single trip. Suite numbers tell you where to go.

  • Sheriff's Office, Suite 101 (270-692-3051): bills and payments, open Monday to Friday between 8:30 and 4:30.
  • Property Valuation Administrator, Suite 202 (270-692-3401): value, name and address changes, and exemption applications, with the same Monday to Friday hours.
  • County Clerk, Suite 102 (270-692-2651): deed recording and delinquent bills. The clerk's own site lists 8:20 to 4:20 on weekdays and a Saturday morning session.

On its FAQ page the sheriff passes valuation and bill-calculation questions to the PVA and sends anyone asking about delinquent bills, or about buying a lien, to the clerk.

sections.h2: What sets Marion County apart from other central Kentucky counties?
sections.html:
Thin settlement defines Marion County: about 57 residents per square mile across 343 square miles of land. Lawmakers formed it in 1834 out of Washington County and gave it the name of Francis Marion. Washington, Boyle, Casey, Taylor, LaRue and Nelson counties surround it.

Three cities exist here. Lebanon, the seat, is the largest, followed by Loretto and Bradfordsville. Gravel Switch, Nerinx, Raywick and St. Mary are smaller places. Wikipedia notes that planar maps put the state's geographic center about three miles north-northwest of Lebanon near KY 429, though neighboring counties dispute it.

Growth has been slow for a century. The first census after formation, in 1840, counted 11,032 residents; later counts ran 16,887 in 1960 and 17,910 in 1980. The tally was 15,499 in 1930, 16,499 in 1990, 18,212 in 2000, 19,820 in 2010 and 19,581 in 2020. By July 2025 the estimate stood at 20,115, a 2.8 percent rise over the 2020 base.

One school district, Marion County Schools, serves every address, with Marion County High School as its comprehensive high school. The Marion County Public Library is in Lebanon. A farm sale has a wrinkle: cropland and pasture are appraised on farm-use value under constitutional Section 172A, while barns and fences are priced at replacement cost minus depreciation.

sections.h2: How do households in Marion County look in the Census data?
sections.html:
Marion County households are settled. More than nine in ten residents were at the same address a year earlier, and owners outnumber renters by more than three to one.

Owners who have paid off their loans spend a median of $415 a month on housing costs. The typical household earns $59,627, and one resident in six lives in poverty. Roughly 87 percent of adults finished high school, while about 15 percent went on to a bachelor's degree. A typical commute runs 22.4 minutes. Veterans total 1,026. The county's 353 employer establishments paid $380.7 million in 2023, and they sit alongside 1,354 firms with no payroll.

Services dominate the economy. In 2022, health care and social assistance took in $110.1 million, lodging and restaurants $25.7 million, and transportation and warehousing $22.0 million, with $230.8 million spent in stores. Residents under 18 make up 22.3 percent of the total, 15.3 percent of people under 65 report a disability, and 86.3 percent of homes have a broadband subscription. Density was 57.8 per square mile in 2010 and 57.1 in 2020, and 57.3 percent of people 16 and older are working or looking for work.

sections.h2: What is the sheriff's collection calendar in Marion County?
sections.html:
Per the sheriff's FAQ, bills are mailed before October 1. Anyone still empty-handed on October 10 should phone for a copy.

  • Oct. 1 to Nov. 1: take two percent off.
  • Nov. 2 to Dec. 31: pay the printed amount.
  • All of January: five percent is added.
  • Feb. 1 to Apr. 15: twenty-one percent is added.

On April 16 whatever remains unpaid shifts to the County Clerk. The twenty-one percent adds the ten percent penalty of KRS 134.015 to the sheriff's collection add-on.

A mailed check should carry the bill number, and a stamped return envelope gets you a receipt. Cards work only at the counter, and the card company's charge falls on the cardholder. The system will not track a partial payment, so send the whole amount at once.

sections.h2: What happens to the bill when a Marion County house sells?
sections.html:
Whoever held the property on January 1 is named on that year's bill. After a sale, the sheriff expects the seller to send the bill on to the buyer, and a buyer left without one can ask the office for a copy. The office adds that it carries no responsibility when a bill is missed during a closing.

Mortgage servicers are not sent a copy. The homeowner receives every bill and must hand it to the lender on time.

For earlier years, call the clerk at 270-692-2651. Overdue bills are transferred there, and the clerk's site advertises a free Online Deed Room. Under KRS 134.420 a tax lien can sit against the land for eleven years, and a title company will want it paid out of the seller's proceeds.

sections.h2: How does a Marion County owner argue with the PVA's number?
sections.html:
Phone 270-692-3401 and request a sit-down. State law makes that meeting the first rung of any appeal, and KRS 133.120 then sends an unresolved case to the clerk as a written petition and on to a hearing. KRS 133.030 opens that hearing between 25 and 35 days after inspection wraps up.

State guidance has PVA staff inspect each Marion County parcel in person every four years or sooner, so find out when yours was visited. Appraisals and nearby sales carry weight. Payment stays due on the amount you claim.

sections.h2: What does the homestead exemption do for a Marion County tax bill?
sections.html: It removes $49,100 from the assessed value for 2025 and 2026. Applied to the county's median home value of $168,100, the taxable base becomes $119,000. The PVA takes applications from owners who are 65 or older or totally disabled and who live in the house. Since 19.5 percent of Marion County residents are 65 or older, the exemption reaches a sizable share of owners. It stays with the owner, so a buyer applies separately.

sections.h2: What happens at the Marion County Clerk's counter when I record a deed?
sections.html: The clerk first collects the grantor's transfer tax, which KRS 142.050 sets at fifty cents for every $500 of value or part of $500. A $168,100 sale produces a charge of $168.50. Taxes paid at the clerk's counter can use cash, check, debit or credit card, and the clerk's site warns that cards carry extra fees. Foreclosure sales, divorce transfers between spouses and parent-to-child deeds for nominal value are exempt.

faqs.q: Where is the Marion County Sheriff's tax office?
faqs.a: It is at 223 North Spalding Avenue, Suite 101, in Lebanon, phone 270-692-3051. Mailed payments should show the bill number.

faqs.q: How much extra does a Marion County bill cost in February?
faqs.a: The sheriff lists a 21 percent penalty from February 1 to April 15, after 5 percent in January. Bills still open on April 16 go to the clerk.

faqs.q: Does the Marion County sheriff accept partial tax payments?
faqs.a: The sheriff's FAQ says its system does not track partial payments, so send the full bill in one payment.

faqs.q: Which office handles Marion County exemptions?
faqs.a: The PVA, at 270-692-3401. The sheriff refers homestead and disability questions there.

faqs.q: Where do I look up a Marion County delinquent bill?
faqs.a: Call the County Clerk at 270-692-2651. Delinquent bills are transferred to that office, and the clerk's site runs a free Online Deed Room.
